final_proof:
Under the standard topological definition, a family of subsets is discrete if every point has a neighborhood meeting at most one member of the family. With this meaning, the claim as stated is false: the hypotheses neither specify a topology on X nor require the sections of the relations V_m to be neighborhoods. This omission cannot be repaired merely by assuming, as the title suggests, that X is T3.

Counterexample. Let X = {0} ∪ {1/k : k is a positive integer}, with the subspace topology inherited from the real line. This is a metrizable, hence T3, space. Put x_0 = 0 and x_k = 1/k for k ≥ 1, and well-order X by x_i ≼ x_j if and only if i ≤ j. For every m ∈ N, let V_m = Δ_X. Then every V_m contains the diagonal and is symmetric, and, for m > 0,

V_m ◦ V_m = Δ_X ⊆ V_{m-1}.

Also U_n = V_n ◦ ⋯ ◦ V_1 = Δ_X for every n > 0. Consequently, for every x ∈ X,

A_n(x) = U_n[x] ∖ ⋃_{y ≺ x} U_{n+1}[y] = {x} ∖ ⋃_{y ≺ x}{y} = {x}.

Thus 𝒜_n is the family of all singleton subsets of X. Every neighborhood of 0 contains 1/k for all sufficiently large k, so it meets infinitely many distinct members of 𝒜_n. Hence 𝒜_n is not discrete. This disproves the claim as written.

A sufficient—and evidently intended—correction is to assume that X is a topological space and that, for every m > 0 and z ∈ X, the section

V_m[z] = {w ∈ X : (z,w) ∈ V_m}

is a neighborhood of z. For example, this follows if each V_m is open in X × X and contains Δ_X. Under this added hypothesis, the claimed conclusion is true.

Proof of the corrected claim. Use the standard convention that (x,t) ∈ R ◦ S exactly when there is s with (x,s) ∈ S and (s,t) ∈ R. Fix n > 0 and z ∈ X. We show that the neighborhood V_{n+2}[z] meets at most one member of 𝒜_n.

Suppose that it meets both A_n(p) and A_n(q), and choose

a ∈ V_{n+2}[z] ∩ A_n(p),    b ∈ V_{n+2}[z] ∩ A_n(q).

If p and q index distinct members, then p ≠ q. Since ≼ is a well-order, it is in particular a total order; after interchanging p with q and a with b if necessary, assume p ≺ q. We have (z,a) ∈ V_{n+2} and (z,b) ∈ V_{n+2}. Symmetry of V_{n+2} gives (a,z) ∈ V_{n+2}, and therefore

(a,b) ∈ V_{n+2} ◦ V_{n+2} ⊆ V_{n+1}.

Moreover, a ∈ A_n(p) ⊆ U_n[p], so (p,a) ∈ U_n. From the definition of U_n,

U_{n+1} = V_{n+1} ◦ U_n.

Combining (p,a) ∈ U_n with (a,b) ∈ V_{n+1} yields (p,b) ∈ U_{n+1}, or equivalently b ∈ U_{n+1}[p]. But p ≺ q, so U_{n+1}[p] is one of the sets removed in the definition

A_n(q) = U_n[q] ∖ ⋃_{y ≺ q} U_{n+1}[y].

It follows that b ∉ A_n(q), contradicting the choice of b. Thus V_{n+2}[z] meets at most one member of 𝒜_n. Since V_{n+2}[z] is a neighborhood of the arbitrary point z, 𝒜_n is discrete. As n > 0 was arbitrary, this holds for every n > 0 under the corrected hypothesis.
